claims.text: The equiatomic quinary Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy exhibits superior strain hardening relative to its equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets.
The quinary alloy exhibits delayed failure relative to its quaternary and ternary subsets.
All compared alloy variants are single-phase FCC after identical thermomechanical processing.
The greater chemical complexity of the quinary alloy promotes more pronounced short-range-order clusters.
Short-range-order clusters stabilize robust solute atmospheres around moving dislocations.
Short-range order and solute atmospheres jointly pin moving dislocations and reduce their mobility.
The proposed pinning mechanism produces a higher density of pinned dislocations during deformation.
Slower dislocation motion and higher pinned-dislocation density increase work hardening.
The increased work hardening produced by this mechanism delays failure.
Removing one or two constituents reduces chemical complexity and consequently diminishes short-range-order development.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary alloys will have higher dislocation mobility.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary alloys will have lower densities of pinned dislocations.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary alloys will show weaker short-range-order signatures.
Stronger short-range-order correlations in the quinary alloy will be associated with enhanced strain hardening.
The comparison will hold thermomechanical history, FCC phase state, temperature, and strain-rate conditions constant while varying constituent count.
The hypothesis is restricted to identically processed, single-phase FCC alloys deformed at room temperature under controlled strain rates.
Separating the quantitative contributions of short-range order and solute-atmosphere pinning may be difficult, and resolution limits may obscure subtle ordering differences.

The mechanism would be falsified if the quinary alloy shows neither significantly reduced dislocation mobility and increased pinned-dislocation density nor a significantly different short-range-order signature from the reduced-component alloys.
